statements.proof_tex:
Write
\[
\mathcal R_{n,d}(\rho)=
\inf_{\widetilde\theta_n}
\sup_{(P_{0,n},P_{1,n})\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\{E(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_n)^2\}^{1/2}.
\]
We prove the upper and lower inequalities separately.

First we record the relation between the causal endpoint and the radius used to define the statistical class.  For a fixed \(z\), let
\[
F_{a,z}(y)=\int_0^yq_{a,n}(v,z)\,dv,
\qquad Q_{a,z}=F_{a,z}^{-1},
\qquad H_z=F_{1,z}-F_{0,z}.
\]
The inverses exist and are continuous because
\(q_{a,n}\ge c>0\) by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\text{-}density\text{-}bounds}\).
The increasing coupling \((Q_{0,z}(U),Q_{1,z}(U))\), with \(U\) uniform, minimizes squared cost: indeed, whenever \(x\le x'\) and \(y\le y'\), direct expansion gives
\[
(x-y)^2+(x'-y')^2
\le (x-y')^2+(x'-y)^2.
\]
Successive uncrossing therefore gives the one-dimensional formula
\[
W_2^2\{Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\}
=\int_0^1\{Q_{1,z}(v)-Q_{0,z}(v)\}^2\,dv.                 \tag{1}
\]
Let \(u_z=\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n(\cdot,z)\).  Since
\(\int_0^1\Delta_n(y,z)\,dy=0\), integration of the defining Neumann equation from \(0\) to \(y\) gives
\[
-\bar q_n(y,z)u_z'(y)=H_z(y).                              \tag{2}
\]
The boundary term vanishes because \(H_z(0)=H_z(1)=0\).  A second integration by parts consequently yields
\[
\int_0^1\Delta_n(y,z)u_z(y)\,dy
=\int_0^1\bar q_n(y,z)\{u_z'(y)\}^2\,dy
=\int_0^1\frac{H_z(y)^2}{\bar q_n(y,z)}\,dy.              \tag{3}
\]
For every \(v\in(0,1)\), the mean-value theorem and
\(F_{a,z}\{Q_{a,z}(v)\}=v\) give a point \(\zeta_{v,z}\) between the two quantiles such that
\[
H_z\{Q_{0,z}(v)\}
=q_{1,n}(\zeta_{v,z},z)\{Q_{0,z}(v)-Q_{1,z}(v)\}.          \tag{4}
\]
Changing variables \(v=F_{0,z}(y)\) in (1), and then using
\(c\le q_{a,n},\bar q_n\le C\) in (3)--(4), proves
\[
\frac{c^2}{C^2}
\int_0^1\Delta_n\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n\,dy
\le W_2^2\{Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\}
\le
\frac{C^2}{c^2}
\int_0^1\Delta_n\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n\,dy.            \tag{5}
\]
The common-marginal assumption permits integration of (5) against the single measure \(R_n\).  By the definitions of \(\rho_n\) and \(\theta_n\), followed by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}local\text{-}equality\text{-}radius}\),
\[
\frac{c^2}{C^2}\rho_n^2\le\theta_n
\le\frac{C^2}{c^2}\rho_n^2
\le\frac{C^2}{c^2}\rho^2.                                \tag{6}
\]
Thus the identically zero estimator has uniform root-mean-square risk at most \((C^2/c^2)\rho^2\).

Put
\[
g_n=n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)},
\qquad
p_n=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{2+a_y}
+\rho^{2a_y/(2+3/s_y+d/s_z)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^2.
\]
The exact expansion in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\text{-}second\text{-}order\text{-}expansion}\)
uses the observable sample map in
\(\mathrm{def{:}anisotropic\text{-}estimator}\) and gives
\(V_{L,n}\lesssim\rho_n^2\), with no reverse-variance premise.  At the resolutions in
\(\mathrm{def{:}anisotropic\text{-}tuning}\), it therefore gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{an}}_{J_y^*,J_z^*,n}-\theta_n\|_2
\lesssim \rho n^{-1/2}+g_n+p_n.                            \tag{7}
\]
For every fixed \(0<\tau<\min\{s_y,s_z\}\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}anisotropic\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}median\text{-}envelope}\)
gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n\|_2
\le C_\tau n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau}.                  \tag{8}
\]
When \(s_z\ge1\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}direct\text{-}cot\text{-}median\text{-}envelope}\)
similarly gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{dir,med}}-\theta_n\|_2
\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{1+1/(d+2)}.                 \tag{9}
\]
For fixed class indices, choose before observing the sample the estimator whose deterministic guarantee among (6)--(9) is smallest.  This is one data-dependent map with a law-independent choice.  Absorbing its fixed constants into \(C_{1,\tau}\) proves the displayed upper bound for \(\mathcal R_{n,d}(\rho)\).

We next prove the converse.  At the resolution
\(2^{J_z}\asymp n^{2/(4s_z+d)}\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}explicit\text{-}mixture\text{-}checks}\) places the null and every component of
\(\mathrm{def{:}rademacher\text{-}family}\) in the same class.  By decreasing the fixed \(c_0\), if necessary, that lemma gives constants \(\eta<1\) and \(c_M>0\) such that
\[
\chi^2(\overline{\mathbb P}_n,\mathbb P_n^0)\le\eta,
\qquad
\theta_n(\omega)-\theta_n(0)
\ge c_M\min\{\rho^2,r_{n,d}(s_z)\}.                        \tag{10}
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the mixture likelihood ratio gives
\[
\|\overline{\mathbb P}_n-\mathbb P_n^0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le\frac12\chi^2(\overline{\mathbb P}_n,\mathbb P_n^0)^{1/2}
\le\frac12\sqrt\eta.                                      \tag{11}
\]
Given any estimator, threshold it halfway between the null endpoint and the lower endpoint separation in (10).  On either testing error its absolute estimation error is at least half that separation.  Averaging the alternative risks over \(\omega\), using (11), and using
\(E|X|\le\{E(X^2)\}^{1/2}\), yields
\[
\mathcal R_{n,d}(\rho)
\ge c_2\min\{\rho^2,r_{n,d}(s_z)\}.                        \tag{12}
\]

It remains to obtain the regular term.  Extend the symmetric cosine family in
\(\mathrm{def{:}no\text{-}covariate\text{-}witness}\) constantly in \(z\), and denote its endpoint by \(\Theta(t)\).  Here
\(\Delta_t(y)=t\cos(2\pi y)\), \(\bar q_t=1\), and direct solution of the Neumann equation gives
\[
\mathcal G\Delta_t(y)=\frac{t}{4\pi^2}\cos(2\pi y),
\qquad
\rho(t)^2=\int_0^1\Delta_t\mathcal G\Delta_t\,dy
=\frac{t^2}{8\pi^2}.                                        \tag{13}
\]
For \(\rho\ge K n^{-1/2}\), choose fixed sufficiently small positive constants and set
\[
t=c_7\min\{\rho,t_0\},
\qquad t'=t+c_8n^{-1/2}.                                    \tag{14}
\]
Equation (13) shows that both laws have radius at most \(\rho\) once \(c_7,c_8\) are small and \(K\) is large.  Positivity, normalization, H\"older membership, and bounded product Hellinger distance follow from
\(\mathrm{ass{:}holder\text{-}radius\text{-}interior}\) and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}explicit\text{-}mixture\text{-}checks}\).

Implicit differentiation of
\(F_{a,t}\{Q_{a,t}(v)\}=v\) gives
\[
\partial_tQ_{a,t}(v)
=-\frac{(2a-1)\sin\{2\pi Q_{a,t}(v)\}}
{4\pi q_{a,t}^{0}\{Q_{a,t}(v)\}}.                         \tag{15}
\]
The denominator is uniformly bounded below.  Thus (15) and dominated differentiation make \(\Theta''\) continuous near zero.  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}cosine\text{-}second\text{-}variation}\),
\(\Theta'(0)=0\) and \(\Theta''(0)=1/(4\pi^2)\).  Shrinking \(t_0\) if necessary, the mean-value theorem applied first to \(\Theta'\) and then to \(\Theta\) gives
\[
|\Theta(t')-\Theta(t)|
\ge c_3\min\{\rho,t_0\}n^{-1/2}
\ge c_3t_0\rho n^{-1/2},                                  \tag{16}
\]
where the last inequality uses \(0\le\rho\le1\).  The two-point testing argument used above, now with the Hellinger affinity supplied by the mixture-check lemma, proves
\[
\mathcal R_{n,d}(\rho)\ge c_4\rho n^{-1/2}
\quad\text{whenever }\rho\ge K n^{-1/2}.                   \tag{17}
\]

Set \(r=r_{n,d}(s_z)=n^{-b}\), where
\(b=4s_z/(4s_z+d)<1\).  If \(\rho<K n^{-1/2}\), then, uniformly for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\(\rho^2\le K^2n^{-1}=o(r)\), so (12) is of order \(\rho^2\), which equals the target minimum.  If \(\rho\ge K n^{-1/2}\) and \(\rho^2\le r\), (12) again supplies \(\rho^2\).  Finally, if \(\rho\ge K n^{-1/2}\) and \(\rho^2>r\), (12) and (17) imply a lower bound by a constant times
\(\max\{r,\rho n^{-1/2}\}\), which is at least half of
\(r+\rho n^{-1/2}\).  In all three cases,
\[
\mathcal R_{n,d}(\rho)
\gtrsim
\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+r_{n,d}(s_z)\}
=\mathfrak R_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho).                           \tag{18}
\]
This proves the lower inequality.

For completeness, we verify the claimed strict gap and phase boundaries.  Write
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}=(\log n/n)^e,
\qquad
e=\frac{1}{2+s_y^{-1}+ds_z^{-1}}.
\]
Because \(d\ge1\) and \(s_y,s_z>0\),
\[
e<\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d}<\frac{2s_z}{4s_z+d}.                  \tag{19}
\]
The polynomial exponent of \(g_n\) is
\((2s_z+ed)/(2s_z+d)\), and direct subtraction gives
\[
\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d}-\frac{2s_z+ed}{2s_z+d}
=\frac{d\{2s_z-e(4s_z+d)\}}
{(4s_z+d)(2s_z+d)}>0.                                       \tag{20}
\]
The logarithmic factor in \(g_n\) has positive power, so (20) proves
\[
n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}=o(g_n).                                  \tag{21}
\]
Since \(x\mapsto x/(2x+d+1)\) is strictly increasing and \(\tau<s_z\),
\[
a_\tau<\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d+1}
<\min\left\{\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d},\frac12\right\}.         \tag{22}
\]
When \(s_z\ge1\), direct cross-multiplication also gives
\[
\frac1{d+2}<\min\left\{\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d},\frac12\right\}. \tag{23}
\]
Thus the global fallbacks can sharpen the upper envelope but do not establish the intrinsic quadratic exponent.

Finally, solving \(\rho_{Q,n}^2=r_{n,d}(s_z)\) and
\(\rho_{L,n}n^{-1/2}=r_{n,d}(s_z)\) gives
\[
\rho_{Q,n}=n^{-2s_z/(4s_z+d)},
\qquad
\rho_{L,n}=n^{(d-4s_z)/\{2(4s_z+d)\}}.                     \tag{24}
\]
The second boundary tends to zero exactly when \(s_z>d/4\).  If \(s_z<d/4\), the intrinsic quadratic lower scale is slower than \(n^{-1/2}\); at the equality boundary the first derivative vanishes by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}cosine\text{-}second\text{-}variation}\).  At \(s_z=d/4\), that lower scale is \(n^{-1/2}\) but still arises from the degenerate quadratic component rather than a positive first-order variance.  Hence for \(s_z\le d/4\) no uniformly positive-variance root-\(n\) description covers the boundary.  Equations (6)--(24) prove every assertion of the theorem.

statements.statement:
Assume \(L>1\). When \(d=0\), use the no-covariate growing-outcome-resolution construction rather than setting \(d=0\) in the conditional tuning rule. Uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{n,0}(s_y,s_z,\rho)\),
\[
\inf_{\widetilde\theta_n}\sup_{(P_{0,n},P_{1,n})\in\mathcal M_{n,0}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}\{E(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_n)^2\}^{1/2}\asymp\mathfrak R_{n,0}(s_y,s_z,\rho)=\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}\}.
\]
At equality under the uniform density, the full-sample bias-retaining estimator has the exact benchmark
\[
n\widehat\theta^0_{J_y^0,n}\Rightarrow2\int_0^1\mathbb B(t)^2dt=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi^2k^2}\xi_{1,k}^2,
\]
where \(J_y^0\to\infty\), \(2^{J_y^0}=o(n)\), and \(2^{-2(s_y+1)J_y^0}=o(n^{-1})\). Subtracting \(2\sum_{k\le2^{J_y^0}}(\pi^2k^2)^{-1}/n\) yields the centered chaos. Thus the outcome resolution genuinely grows, the quadratic scale is \(n^{-1}\), and \(\rho_{Q,n}=\rho_{L,n}=n^{-1/2}\). This is the two-sample specialization of the del Barrio--Gin\'e--Utzet weighted quantile-process law.
statements.justification: A separate full-sample estimator is necessary to recover the classical two-sample constant rather than a split-sample direct-sum surrogate.
statements.gap: delBarrioGineUtzet2005 gives the unconditional quantile-process limit but not its role as the \(d=0\) branch of a conditional smoothness--degeneracy frontier.
statements.consumer: The result is the required sanity check and supplies exact simulation critical values when no covariate adjustment is used.
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(d=0\).  For arm \(a\), write \(F_a\) for the distribution function, \(Q_a=F_a^{-1}\),
\[
D=Q_1-Q_0,
\qquad
\widehat D=\widehat Q_{1,n}-\widehat Q_{0,n},
\qquad
P_J=P^Q_{J_y}.
\]
The uncrossing calculation in the proof of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}conditional\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\) gives the one-dimensional identity
\[
\theta_n=\int_0^1D(u)^2\,du=\|D\|_2^2,                     \tag{1}
\]
whereas
\(\mathrm{def{:}no\text{-}covariate\text{-}branch}\) defines the explicit sample map
\[
\widehat\theta^0_{J_y,n}=\|P_J\widehat D\|_2^2.            \tag{2}
\]

We first establish its uniform risk.  Since \(q_{a,n}\ge c\), every \(Q_a\) is \(c^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.  Under the probability integral transform, for almost every \(u\in(0,1)\),
\[
\widehat Q_{a,n}(u)=Q_a\{U_{a,(k)}\},
\qquad k=\lceil nu\rceil,
\]
where \(U_{a,(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th order statistic of \(n\) independent uniform variables.  Its density is proportional to
\(x^{k-1}(1-x)^{n-k}\).  Integrating this beta density gives, for \(j=1,2,3,4\),
\[
E\{U_{a,(k)}^j\}
=\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}\frac{k+r}{n+1+r}.                       \tag{3}
\]
Because \(|k/(n+1)-u|\le2/n\), expanding the centered powers in (3) gives universal constants such that
\[
\sup_{a,u}E|U_{a,(k)}-u|^2\le\frac{C_2}{n},
\qquad
\sup_{a,u}E|U_{a,(k)}-u|^4\le\frac{C_4}{n^2}.              \tag{4}
\]
The Lipschitz property, Tonelli's theorem, Jensen's inequality, and
\(|x-y|^j\le2^{j-1}(|x|^j+|y|^j)\) now yield
\[
E\|\widehat D-D\|_2^2\lesssim n^{-1},
\qquad
E\|\widehat D-D\|_2^4\lesssim n^{-2}.                    \tag{5}
\]

The identity \(Q_a'=1/(q_{a,n}\circ Q_a)\), the lower density bound, and the composition and product rules for H\"older differences show inductively that
\(Q_a\in\mathcal C^{s_y+1}([0,1])\), with norm bounded only by \((c,C,L,s_y)\).  The boundary wavelets in
\(\mathrm{ass{:}wavelet\text{-}regularity}\) have regularity beyond \(s_y+1\); Taylor expansion against their vanishing moments therefore bounds a level-\(j\) coefficient by a constant times
\(2^{-j(s_y+3/2)}\).  Summing the squared coefficients above \(J_y\) gives
\[
\|(I-P_J)D\|_2^2\lesssim2^{-2(s_y+1)J_y}.                  \tag{6}
\]
Let \(E_J=P_J(\widehat D-D)\) and \(B_J=(I-P_J)D\).  Orthogonality gives the exact decomposition
\[
\widehat\theta^0_{J_y,n}-\theta_n
=2\langle P_JD,E_J\rangle+\|E_J\|_2^2-\|B_J\|_2^2.        \tag{7}
\]
Since \(P_J\) is a contraction, (5)--(7) and Cauchy--Schwarz imply
\[
\|\widehat\theta^0_{J_y,n}-\theta_n\|_{L^2(P)}
\lesssim
\|D\|_2n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}+2^{-2(s_y+1)J_y}.                  \tag{8}
\]
The energy comparison (5) in the preceding proof applies also when \(d=0\), and hence
\(\|D\|_2^2=\theta_n\lesssim\rho_n^2\le\rho^2\).  At \(J_y=J_y^0\), the tuning condition in
\(\mathrm{def{:}no\text{-}covariate\text{-}branch}\) makes the last term in (8) \(o(n^{-1})\), so
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,0}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta^0_{J_y^0,n}-\theta_n\|_2
\lesssim\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}.                              \tag{9}
\]
The zero estimator and the same energy comparison give the additional bound \(O(\rho^2)\).  Choosing the better deterministic guarantee proves the minimax upper bound.

For the converse, use the fixed-frequency laws in
\(\mathrm{def{:}no\text{-}covariate\text{-}witness}\).  First compare \(t=0\) with
\[
t'=c_0\min\{\rho,n^{-1/2}\}.                               \tag{10}
\]
For sufficiently small \(c_0\), both laws are in the class by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}explicit\text{-}mixture\text{-}checks}\), and their product Hellinger distance is bounded away from its maximal value.  The expansion in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}cosine\text{-}second\text{-}variation}\), with continuity of the second derivative obtained by implicit differentiation of the quantiles, gives endpoint separation
\[
|\Theta(t')-\Theta(0)|\gtrsim\min\{\rho^2,n^{-1}\}.        \tag{11}
\]
If \(\rho\ge K n^{-1/2}\), compare instead
\[
t=c_1\rho,
\qquad t'=c_1\rho+c_2n^{-1/2},                              \tag{12}
\]
where \(c_1,c_2\) are fixed and small and \(K\) is fixed and large.  The exact radius calculation
\(\rho(t)=|t|/(2\sqrt2\pi)\) puts both points in the class.  The derivative calculation (15) in the preceding proof and
\(\Theta''(0)=1/(4\pi^2)\) imply, after making \(c_1\) small, that
\[
|\Theta(t')-\Theta(t)|\gtrsim\rho n^{-1/2}.                 \tag{13}
\]
Thresholding any estimator halfway between the two endpoints, the testing affinity supplied by the Hellinger bound yields an root-mean-square lower bound by a fixed multiple of (11), and also of (13) in its stated regime.  Splitting at \(\rho=K n^{-1/2}\), exactly as in the three cases leading to (18) above but with \(r=n^{-1}\), gives
\[
\inf_{\widetilde\theta_n}
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,0}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\{E(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_n)^2\}^{1/2}
\gtrsim\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}\}.              \tag{14}
\]
Together, (9), the zero-estimator bound, and (14) prove the minimax equivalence.

It remains to identify the exact equality limit.  Under the uniform density, define
\[
u_{a,n}(t)=\sqrt n\{t-\widehat Q_{a,n}(t)\},
\qquad
u_{a,n}^{\mathrm{tr}}(t)=u_{a,n}(t)\mathbf1\{1/n<t<1-1/n\}.
\]
By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}del\text{-}barrio\text{-}gine\text{-}utzet\text{-}uniform\text{-}quantile\text{-}limit}\),
\(u_{a,n}^{\mathrm{tr}}\Rightarrow\mathbb B_a\) in \(L^2(0,1)\).  Formula (3) for the first and last order statistics gives
\[
E\|u_{a,n}-u_{a,n}^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_2^2=O(n^{-2}),          \tag{15}
\]
so the same convergence holds for \(u_{a,n}\).  Independence of the arm samples in
\(\mathrm{ass{:}two\text{-}arm\text{-}sampling}\) gives joint convergence to independent bridges.  Consequently,
\[
X_n:=\sqrt n(\widehat Q_{1,n}-\widehat Q_{0,n})
=u_{0,n}-u_{1,n}
\Rightarrow\mathbb B_0-\mathbb B_1
\stackrel{d}=\sqrt2\,\mathbb B                              \tag{16}
\]
in \(L^2(0,1)\).

Because \(J_y^0\to\infty\), the orthogonal projectors
\(P^Q_{J_y^0}\) converge strongly to the identity.  Strong convergence of uniformly bounded operators is uniform on compact subsets of \(L^2\): this follows by covering a compact set by finitely many small balls and using the contraction property.  Tightness in (16) therefore gives
\[
\|(I-P^Q_{J_y^0})X_n\|_2=o_P(1).                           \tag{17}
\]
Equations (2), (16), and (17), followed by continuity of the squared norm, yield
\[
n\widehat\theta^0_{J_y^0,n}
=\|P^Q_{J_y^0}X_n\|_2^2
\Rightarrow2\int_0^1\mathbb B(t)^2\,dt.                   \tag{18}
\]
The covariance kernel \(s\wedge t-st\) is the Green kernel of the Dirichlet operator \(-d^2/dt^2\).  Direct differentiation verifies the normalized eigenfunctions
\(\sqrt2\sin(\pi kt)\) and eigenvalues \((\pi^2k^2)^{-1}\).  Expanding the Gaussian bridge in that orthonormal basis gives
\[
2\int_0^1\mathbb B(t)^2\,dt
=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi^2k^2}\xi_{1,k}^2.        \tag{19}
\]
Moreover,
\(2\sum_{k\le2^{J_y^0}}(\pi^2k^2)^{-1}\to
2\sum_{k\ge1}(\pi^2k^2)^{-1}=1/3\).  Thus subtracting the stated finite sum divided by \(n\) from \(\widehat\theta^0_{J_y^0,n}\) changes the limit in (19) to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi^2k^2}(\xi_{1,k}^2-1),
\]
the centered chaos.  Finally, equating \(\rho^2\), \(\rho n^{-1/2}\), and \(n^{-1}\) gives
\(\rho_{Q,n}=\rho_{L,n}=n^{-1/2}\), as claimed.

statements.statement:
Can the mixed linear--quadratic calibration handle construct \(\mathcal I_n^{\mathrm{mix}}\) such that
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{0\le\rho\le1}\inf_{(P_{0,n},P_{1,n})\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}P\{\theta_n\in\mathcal I_n^{\mathrm{mix}}\}\ge1-\alpha,
\]
with expected half-width, at the corrected resolutions for \(d\ge1\), of order
\[
\rho n^{-1/2}
+n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}
+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{2+a_y}
+\rho^{2a_y/(2+3/s_y+d/s_z)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^2,
\]
and of order \(\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}\) for \(d=0\)?  At each fixed unequal law, can the same construction attain the regular Gaussian width whenever the corrected pilot remainder is \(o(n^{-1/2})\)? The construction must derive from the primitive model class uniform spectral-tail, anti-concentration, common-multiplier coupling, observable pilot-Hessian and covariance control, and a valid allowance for the corrected pilot remainder
\[
C_B\left[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\{2^{-(s_y+1)J_y}+\mathbf 1\{d\ge1\}2^{-s_zJ_z}\}
+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{2+a_y}
+\rho^{2a_y/(2+3/s_y+d/s_z)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^2
\right].
\]
No centering by \(B^y_{J_y,n}+B^z_{J_z,n}\) is permitted.
statements.justification: Uniform observable calibration remains the genuine unresolved step after correcting the point-estimator expansion and width.
statements.gap: The population Gaussianization theorem does not establish observable common-multiplier quantile consistency or anti-concentration through variance degeneracy.
statements.consumer: A positive answer would provide one defensible uncertainty report for the \(\mathsf{STAR}\) conditional bound across null, local, and regular regimes.

statements.statement: Let \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) be independent uniform random variables on \((0,1)\), let \(G_n^{-1}\) be their empirical quantile function, set \(u_n(t)=\sqrt n\{t-G_n^{-1}(t)\}\), and define \(u_n^{\mathrm{tr}}(t)=u_n(t)\mathbf 1\{1/n<t<1-1/n\}\).  Then \(u_n^{\mathrm{tr}}\Rightarrow\mathbb B\) weakly in \(L^2(0,1)\), where \(\mathbb B\) is a standard Brownian bridge.

statements.statement:
For \(d\ge1\), specialize Definition 4 and Theorem 4 of Lin, Gao, Blanchet, and Glynn to scalar outcomes, \(d\)-dimensional covariates, group sizes \(n_0,n_1\), and \(N=n_0\wedge n_1\).  If the outcome and covariate supports are compact, the transport objective is Lipschitz, both conditional kernels are Wasserstein--1 Lipschitz in the covariate, the two arm samples are independent and i.i.d. within arm, and the estimator's covariate coupling obeys
\[
E\!\left[\int\|z_0-z_1\|_2\,d\widehat\pi_{n_0,n_1}(z_0,z_1)\right]\le C_{\widehat\pi}N^{-1/(d+2)},
\]
then its adapted direct conditional-optimal-transport estimator and population value satisfy
\[
E|\widehat V_{n_0,n_1}-V_{\mathrm c}|\le \overline C N^{-1/(d+2)}\log N.
\]

source.verbatim_statement: Under Assp. 4--9 with \(r=1/(d_Z+2\vee d_Y)\), \[\mathbb E[|\widehat V_{n_0,n_1}-V_{\mathrm c}|]\le\overline C\gamma_{d_Y,d_Z}(n_0\wedge n_1),\] where \[\gamma_{d_Y,d_Z}(N)=\begin{cases}N^{-1/(d_Z+2\vee d_Y)}\log N,&d_Y\ne2,\\N^{-1/(d_Z+2\vee d_Y)},&d_Y=2.\end{cases}\]

statements.statement:
Fix \(d\ge1\), \(\tau>0\), and a block size \(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\). Suppose the two joint laws on \([0,1]^{d+1}\) have densities \(p_{a,n}\) bounded above and away from zero and belonging to \(\mathcal C^{\tau+\epsilon}([0,1]^{d+1})\) for some \(\epsilon>0\). For the squared-distance cost and the aligned wavelet COT block value \(\widehat V_{\ell,\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}\) at resolution \(J_{\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}=\lfloor\log_2(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})/(2\tau+d+1)\rfloor\), there is a finite constant \(C\), depending on the two laws, their density bound, \(\tau\), and \(d\), such that
\[
E\left|\widehat V_{\ell,\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}-\theta_n\right|
\le C(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{-\tau/(2\tau+d+1)}.
\]

statements.statement:
Let \(d\ge1\) and fix \(0<\tau<\min\{s_y,s_z\}\). Put \(\epsilon_\tau=\{\min(s_y,s_z)-\tau\}/2\), \(a_\tau=\tau/(2\tau+d+1)\), and \(p_{a,n}(y,z)=q_{a,n}(y,z)r_n(z)\). Uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)\),
\[
c^2\le p_{a,n}(y,z)\le C^2,
\qquad
p_{a,n}\in\mathcal C^{\tau+\epsilon_\tau}([0,1]^{d+1}),
\qquad
\sup_{a,n}\|p_{a,n}\|_{\mathcal C^{\tau+\epsilon_\tau}}\le H_\tau<\infty,
\]
where \(H_\tau\) depends only on \((c,C,L,s_y,s_z,d,\tau)\). The explicit estimator in \(\mathrm{def{:}smoothcot\text{-}median\text{-}estimator}\) then satisfies
\[
\sup_{(P_{0,n},P_{1,n})\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\left\{E(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n)^2\right\}^{1/2}
\le C_\tau n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(C_\tau\) depending only on the same fixed quantities.
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(s_*=\min\{s_y,s_z\}\) and \(\alpha=\tau+\epsilon_\tau=(s_*+\tau)/2<s_*\). By the common-marginal factorization and the density bounds,
\[
p_{a,n}(y,z)=q_{a,n}(y,z)r_n(z),
\qquad c^2\le p_{a,n}(y,z)\le C^2.                                 \tag{1}
\]
We verify the isotropic H\"older inclusion. Let \(k=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\), write a multi-index on \([0,1]^{d+1}\) as \(\mu=(\mu_y,\mu_z)\), and take \(|\mu|\le k\). Since \(k<\alpha<s_*\), every derivative below is licensed by \(\mathrm{ass{:}anisotropic\text{-}conditional\text{-}smoothness}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}covariate\text{-}holder\text{-}smoothness}\). The product rule gives
\[
D^\mu p_{a,n}(y,z)
=\sum_{\nu_z\le\mu_z}{\mu_z\choose\nu_z}
\{D_y^{\mu_y}D_z^{\nu_z}q_{a,n}(y,z)\}
\{D_z^{\mu_z-\nu_z}r_n(z)\}.                                    \tag{2}
\]
Every factor on the right of (2) is uniformly bounded by the radius \(L\), so \(\|D^\mu p_{a,n}\|_\infty\le H_{0,\tau}\), where the constant depends only on \((L,d,k)\). For \(|\mu|=k\), apply the identity \(fg-f'g'=f(g-g')+g'(f-f')\) to each summand in (2), and change the coordinates from \((y,z)\) to \((y',z')\) one at a time. The anisotropic H\"older bounds and \(\alpha<s_y,s_z\) give
\[
|D^\mu p_{a,n}(y,z)-D^\mu p_{a,n}(y',z')|
\le H_{1,\tau}\left(|y-y'|^{\alpha-k}+\sum_{j=1}^d|z_j-z'_j|^{\alpha-k}\right)
\le H_{2,\tau}\|(y,z)-(y',z')\|_2^{\alpha-k}.                    \tag{3}
\]
For integer \(\alpha\), the same coordinate telescoping gives the source's integer-order modulus convention; alternatively one may reduce \(\epsilon_\tau\) by a fixed factor without changing any rate. Equations (2)--(3) are precisely the isotropic \(\mathcal C^\alpha\) norm bound, proving
\[
\sup_{a,n}\|p_{a,n}\|_{\mathcal C^\alpha}\le H_\tau.            \tag{4}
\]

Apply the cited \(\mathrm{lem{:}lin\text{-}gao\text{-}blanchet\text{-}glynn\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}rate}\) with outcome dimension one, covariate dimension \(d\), smoothness parameter \(\tau\), extra smoothness \(\epsilon_\tau\), and squared cost. On \([0,1]^2\),
\[
|(y_1-y_0)^2-(y_1'-y_0')^2|
\le2(|y_0-y_0'|+|y_1-y_1'|),                                      \tag{5}
\]
so its Lipschitz constant is fixed. The theorem's printed constant is law-dependent, so uniformity must be checked rather than assumed. Its proof has three law-dependent inputs: a reciprocal density bound, the joint wavelet \(L^2\) constant, and the high-probability positivity constant. By (1), the first is bounded by \(\max\{c^{-2},C^2\}\). At a generic resolution \(J\), orthogonality, the wavelet characterization of (4), and bounded variance of empirical coefficients give, uniformly in the law,
\[
E\|\widetilde p_{a,J}-p_{a,n}\|_2^2
\le C_\tau\left\{2^{-2\tau J}+\frac{2^{(d+1)J}}{N_n^{\mathrm{sm}}}\right\}. \tag{6}
\]
At \(J=J_{\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}\), both terms in (6) are at most a constant times \((N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{-2a_\tau}\). The positive-part normalization is inactive on the event \(\|\widetilde p_{a,J}-p_{a,n}\|_\infty<c^2/2\). Compact wavelet support, coefficientwise Bernstein inequalities, and a union bound over \(O(2^{(d+1)J})\) coefficients give
\[
P\{\|\widetilde p_{a,J}-p_{a,n}\|_\infty\ge c^2/2\}
\le C_\tau(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{-2},                               \tag{7}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\): the deterministic bias is \(O(2^{-\alpha J})\), while the stochastic sup-norm scale is \(O\{(J2^{(d+1)J}/N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{1/2}\}=o(1)\) because \(\alpha>\tau\). Thus the constants in (6)--(7), and hence the Besov and conditional-density bounds in the cited theorem's proof, are controlled only by \((c,C,H_\tau,\tau,d)\).

For completeness, the only derivative-dependent marginal comparison in the source proof is unnecessary here. If \(f(z)=W_2^2(Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z))\), \(\widehat f\) is its block analogue, and \(\widehat r\) is the aligned block marginal, then \(0\le f,\widehat f\le1\) and
\[
\left|\int\widehat f\,\widehat r-\int f r_n\right|
\le\|\widehat r-r_n\|_1+
2\int\{W_1(\widehat Q_0^z,Q_0^z)+W_1(\widehat Q_1^z,Q_1^z)\}\widehat r(z)\,dz. \tag{8}
\]
The first term is bounded by the joint \(L^2\) error in (6); the second is the conditional negative-order term bounded in the cited proof. Equations (6)--(8) therefore uniformize its conclusion:
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}}
E_P|\widehat V_{\ell,\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}-\theta_n|
\le C_\tau(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{-a_\tau}.                           \tag{9}
\]

Let \(\delta_n=C_\tau(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}})^{-a_\tau}\). Markov's inequality applied to (9) makes a block bad at threshold \(8\delta_n\) with probability at most \(1/8\). Disjoint blocks are independent by \(\mathrm{ass{:}two\text{-}arm\text{-}sampling}\). If the median is bad, at least \((K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}+1)/2\) blocks are bad; hence
\[
P\{|\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n|>8\delta_n\}
\le2^{K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}}8^{-(K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}+1)/2}
\le2^{-K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}/2}.                                      \tag{10}
\]
Choose the fixed multiplier in \(K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\asymp\log n\) so that the last quantity is at most \(\delta_n^2\). Both the estimator and \(\theta_n\) lie in \([0,1]\), so
\[
E(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n)^2
\le64\delta_n^2+2^{-K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}/2}
\le65\delta_n^2.                                                   \tag{11}
\]
Finally, \(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\asymp n/\log n\), and (11) is the asserted root-mean-square rate.

Let \(d\ge1\), \(J_y,J_z\to\infty\), \(D_{J_y,J_z}=o(n^2)\), and let \(n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n}\) be the canonical quadratic projection obtained from the raw-moment Hessian. Put \(M_n=2^{dJ_z}\). After indexing the independent evaluation observations by \(r\), it has an explicit representation \(n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n}=\sum_{r<s}h_{n,rs}(W_r,W_s)\), with each kernel canonical in either argument, such that
\[
\operatorname{Var}(n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})=A_{J_y,J_z,n}^2\{1+o(1)\},
\]
\[
\max_r\sum_{s\ne r}E h_{n,rs}^2\lesssim \frac{M_n}{m},
\qquad
\sum_{r<s}E h_{n,rs}^4\lesssim\frac{M_n^3}{m^2},
\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{tr}(K_{J_y,J_z,n}^4)}{\operatorname{tr}(K_{J_y,J_z,n}^2)^2}\lesssim M_n^{-1}.
\]
If \(G_n=\sum_r\ell_{n,r}(W_r)\) is the projected linear term, its summands are centered and uniformly bounded, \(E G_n^2=O(S_n^2)\), and \(S_n\ge A_{J_y,J_z,n}\), then for the filtration generated by the ordered observations and
\[
\mathcal D_{n,r}=\ell_{n,r}(W_r)+\sum_{s<r}h_{n,sr}(W_s,W_r),
\]
the array is a martingale-difference array and, for every \(\epsilon>0\),
\[
\sum_rE\left[\left(\frac{\mathcal D_{n,r}}{S_n}\right)^2
\mathbf 1\{|\mathcal D_{n,r}|>\epsilon S_n\}\right]\to0,
\]
\[
\frac{E\left[\left\{\sum_rE(\mathcal D_{n,r}^2\mid\mathcal F_{r-1})-E(G_n+n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})^2\right\}^2\right]}{S_n^4}
\lesssim m^{-1}+\frac{M_n}{m^2}+M_n^{-1}+o(1)\to0.
\]
statements.justification: The finite Gaussian-quadratic proxy requires explicit changing-kernel moment and influence controls rather than an undeclared appeal to a generic U-statistic theorem.
statements.gap: The frozen primitives specify the kernel and its spectrum but do not themselves imply fourth-moment contraction, Lindeberg, or predictable conditional-variance bounds.
statements.consumer: The mixed spectral-transition theorem uses this lemma to prove both the finite proxy and forced diffuse Gaussianization.
statements.proof_tex:
Write \(M_n=2^{dJ_z}\), \(B=B_{J_y,J_z,n}\), \(K=K_{J_y,J_z,n}\), and \(A=A_{J_y,J_z,n}\). All constants below depend only on the density bounds, the compactly supported boundary-wavelet bases, and the fixed support dimension, and hence are uniform over the declared model class.

We first control the raw quadratic kernel without assuming that the two Gram conjugations preserve compact support. Replace the covariate wavelets spanning the levels through \(J_z\) by the orthonormal tensor boundary-scaling basis \(\{\varphi_{J_z,k}:k\in\mathcal K_{J_z}^{\mathrm{sc}}\}\) of the same space. This orthogonal coordinate change leaves the scalar kernel \(\Phi(w)^{\top}B\Phi(w')\), its moments, and the eigenvalues of \(K\) unchanged. Its covariate Gram matrix is
\[
G_z(k,l)=\int_{\mathcal Z_d}\varphi_{J_z,k}(v)\varphi_{J_z,l}(v)r_n(v)\,dv. \tag{1}
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass{:}covariate\text{-}density\text{-}bounds}\),
\[
cI\preceq G_z\preceq CI. \tag{2}
\]
By compact support in \(\mathrm{ass{:}wavelet\text{-}regularity}\), there is a fixed integer \(R\) such that \(G_z(k,l)=0\) whenever the lattice distance between \(k\) and \(l\) exceeds \(R\). Put \(a=(C+c)/2\) and \(E=I-G_z/a\). Equation (2) gives
\[
\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le q:=\frac{C-c}{C+c}<1,
\]
whereas bandedness gives \((E^j)_{kl}=0\) if \(\operatorname{dist}(k,l)>Rj\). The norm-convergent Neumann series therefore yields the entrywise inverse localization
\[
|G_z^{-1}(k,l)|
=\left|a^{-1}\sum_{j\ge0}(E^j)_{kl}\right|
\le \frac{a^{-1}}{1-q}q^{\lceil\operatorname{dist}(k,l)/R\rceil}. \tag{3}
\]
Consequently, for
\[
\kappa_{J_z}(z,v)=\sum_{k,l}\varphi_{J_z,k}(z)G_z^{-1}(k,l)\varphi_{J_z,l}(v),
\]
the wavelet sup-norm bound and bounded overlap imply
\[
|\kappa_{J_z}(z,v)|
\le C_0M_n\exp\{-c_0 2^{J_z}\|z-v\|_2\}. \tag{4}
\]

For the outcome coordinate, let \(R^y_{J_y}\) be the kernel of the orthogonal projector onto the retained zero-mean outcome space. Compact support and bounded overlap give
\[
\sup_{J_y,y}\int_{\mathcal Y}|R^y_{J_y}(y,u)|\,du\le C_1. \tag{5}
\]
The Green kernel of \(\mathcal G_{n,z}\) is uniformly bounded. Indeed, if \(u=\mathcal G_{n,z}h\) and \(\int_0^1h=0\), integration of the differential equation and the Neumann boundary condition gives
\[
u'(y)=-\bar q_n(y,z)^{-1}\int_0^yh(v)\,dv.
\]
The lower density bound in \(\mathrm{ass{:}conditional\text{-}density\text{-}bounds}\), followed by the normalization \(\int_0^1u=0\), represents \(u\) as an integral of \(h\) against a kernel bounded only in terms of \(c\). Combining this representation with (5) on both sides of the inverse shows that the kernel \(g_{J_y}(y,y';z)\) of \(P_{J_y}\mathcal G_{n,z}P_{J_y}\) obeys
\[
\sup_{J_y,y,y',z}|g_{J_y}(y,y';z)|\le C_2. \tag{6}
\]

The full projection Gram matrix is the identity on the orthonormal outcome coordinates tensored with \(G_z\). Expanding both Gram inverses in \(\mathrm{def{:}whitened\text{-}spectral\text{-}array}\) therefore gives the exact identity
\[
b_J\{(y,z),(y',z')\}
:=\Phi(y,z)^{\top}B\Phi(y',z')
=\int_{\mathcal Z_d}\kappa_{J_z}(z,v)\kappa_{J_z}(z',v)
g_{J_y}(y,y';v)\,dR_n(v). \tag{7}
\]
Thus both raw-moment Gram conjugations are included. Equations (4), (6), the upper density bound, and \(\|z-v\|_2+\|z'-v\|_2\ge\|z-z'\|_2\) imply
\[
|b_J\{(y,z),(y',z')\}|
\le C_3M_n\exp\{-c_1 2^{J_z}\|z-z'\|_2\}. \tag{8}
\]
Because each joint arm density is at most \(C^2\), integration of (8) over a covariate tube of volume \(O(M_n^{-1})\) gives, for \(p\in\{2,4\}\),
\[
\max_{a,b}\iint|b_J(w,w')|^p\,dP_{a,n}(w)dP_{b,n}(w')
\le C_4M_n^{p-1},
\]
\[
\max_{a,b,w}\int|b_J(w,w')|^p\,dP_{b,n}(w')
\le C_4M_n^{p-1}. \tag{9}
\]
Let \(\mu_a=E_{P_{a,n}}\Phi(W)\) and
\[
b_{ab}^{\circ}(w,w')=
\{\Phi(w)-\mu_a\}^{\top}B\{\Phi(w')-\mu_b\}.
\]
Expanding the two centerings expresses \(b_{ab}^{\circ}\) as the raw kernel minus its two one-coordinate conditional expectations plus its expectation. Jensen's inequality applied to each conditional expectation preserves the orders in (9). Hence
\[
E|b_{ab}^{\circ}(W_a,W_b)|^2\lesssim M_n,
\qquad
E|b_{ab}^{\circ}(W_a,W_b)|^4\lesssim M_n^3, \tag{10}
\]
and the conditional second moment in either argument has \(L^2\)-norm \(O(M_n)\).

We next record the four-cycle contraction. For
\[
c_{abc}(w,w')=E_{P_{c,n}}
\{b_{ac}^{\circ}(w,W_c)b_{bc}^{\circ}(w',W_c)\},
\]
covariance algebra identifies \(\|c_{abc}\|_2^2\) with a cyclic trace containing two factors \(B\Gamma_cB\) and the two exterior arm covariances. Since \(0\preceq\Gamma_a\preceq\Gamma:=\Gamma_0+\Gamma_1\), each exterior factor can be written as a contraction conjugated by \(\Gamma^{1/2}\). Cyclicity of trace and the Hilbert--Schmidt inequality then give
\[
\|c_{abc}\|_2^2\lesssim\operatorname{tr}(K^4).
\]
By \(\mathrm{prop{:}anisotropic\text{-}spectrum\text{-}bias}\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}(K^4)
\le\|K\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\operatorname{tr}(K^2)\lesssim M_n,
\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{tr}(K^4)}{\operatorname{tr}(K^2)^2}\lesssim M_n^{-1}. \tag{11}
\]

Index an evaluation observation by \(r=(e,a,i)\), put \(Z_r=\Phi(W_r)-E\Phi(W_r)\), and order observations fold by fold. Direct expansion of the diagonal-free statistic in \(\mathrm{def{:}anisotropic\text{-}estimator}\), using \(n=2m\), gives
\[
h_{n,rs}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2}{m-1}x^{\top}By,&e_r=e_s,\ a_r=a_s,\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{2}{m}x^{\top}By,&e_r=e_s,\ a_r\ne a_s,\\[4pt]
0,&e_r\ne e_s,
\end{cases}
\qquad
n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n}=\sum_{r<s}h_{n,rs}(Z_r,Z_s). \tag{12}
\]
Independence in \(\mathrm{ass{:}two\text{-}arm\text{-}sampling}\) and \(EZ_r=0\) show that each kernel is canonical in either argument. There are \(O(m)\) nonzero edges incident to a vertex and \(O(m^2)\) nonzero edges in total. Equations (10) and (12) therefore give
\[
\max_r\sum_{s\ne r}Eh_{n,rs}^2\lesssim\frac{M_n}{m},
\qquad
\sum_{r<s}Eh_{n,rs}^4\lesssim\frac{M_n^3}{m^2}. \tag{13}
\]
Canonicality makes distinct edges orthogonal, including two edges sharing exactly one vertex. Summing the edge variances and separating within-arm from cross-arm edges yields
\[
\begin{split}
\operatorname{Var}(n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})
&=\frac{4m}{m-1}\sum_{a=0}^1\operatorname{tr}(B\Gamma_aB\Gamma_a)
+8\operatorname{tr}(B\Gamma_0B\Gamma_1)\\
&=4\operatorname{tr}\{B(\Gamma_0+\Gamma_1)B(\Gamma_0+\Gamma_1)\}
+O(m^{-1})\operatorname{tr}(K^2)\\
&=A^2\{1+O(m^{-1})\}.
\end{split} \tag{14}
\]
Here \(A^2=4\operatorname{tr}(K^2)\asymp M_n\) by \(\mathrm{prop{:}anisotropic\text{-}spectrum\text{-}bias}\), proving the variance assertion.

It remains to verify Lindeberg and predictable-variance concentration. Let
\[
q_r=\sum_{s<r}h_{n,sr}(Z_s,Z_r),
\qquad
\mathcal D_{n,r}=\ell_{n,r}(W_r)+q_r.
\]
Canonicality gives \(E(\mathcal D_{n,r}\mid\mathcal F_{r-1})=0\) and \(\sum_r\mathcal D_{n,r}=G_n+n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n}\). Conditional on \(W_r\), the summands in \(q_r\) are independent and centered. Thus
\[
Eq_r^4
=\sum_{s<r}Eh_{n,sr}^4
+6\sum_{s<t<r}E\!\left[E(h_{n,sr}^2\mid W_r)E(h_{n,tr}^2\mid W_r)\right]. \tag{15}
\]
The sectional bound after (10), including the \(O(m^{-1})\) edge coefficients, bounds the sum of conditional second moments in (15) by \(C_5M_n/m\). Summing over \(r\) and applying (13) gives
\[
\sum_rEq_r^4\lesssim\frac{M_n^2}{m}+\frac{M_n^3}{m^2}. \tag{16}
\]
If \(|\ell_{n,r}|\le L_0\), independence and centering imply
\[
\sum_rE\ell_{n,r}^4\le L_0^2\sum_rE\ell_{n,r}^2
=L_0^2EG_n^2=O(S_n^2).
\]
Since \(S_n\ge A\asymp M_n^{1/2}\), (16) and \((x+y)^4\le8(x^4+y^4)\) yield
\[
S_n^{-4}\sum_rE\mathcal D_{n,r}^4
\lesssim M_n^{-1}+m^{-1}+\frac{M_n}{m^2}\longrightarrow0. \tag{17}
\]
Indeed, \(J_z\to\infty\) gives \(M_n\to\infty\), while \(M_n\le D_{J_y,J_z}=o(n^2)=o(m^2)\). For every \(\epsilon>0\), the bound
\[
x^2\mathbf 1\{|x|>\epsilon S_n\}\le\frac{x^4}{\epsilon^2S_n^2}
\]
and (17) prove the stated Lindeberg conclusion after summation and expectation.

Finally, direct expansion gives
\[
\sum_rE(\mathcal D_{n,r}^2\mid\mathcal F_{r-1})
=E(G_n+n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})^2+C_n+R_n+T_n, \tag{18}
\]
where
\[
\begin{split}
C_n&=2\sum_r\sum_{s<r}E\{\ell_{n,r}(W_r)h_{n,sr}(Z_s,Z_r)\mid Z_s\},\\
R_n&=\sum_r\sum_{s<r}\{E(h_{n,sr}^2\mid Z_s)-Eh_{n,sr}^2\},\\
T_n&=2\sum_r\sum_{s<t<r}E\{h_{n,sr}h_{n,tr}\mid Z_s,Z_t\}.
\end{split} \tag{19}
\]
To verify the constant in (18), canonicality gives \(E(G_n\,n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})=0\), and the orthogonality of distinct canonical edges gives \(E(n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})^2=\sum_{r<s}Eh_{n,rs}^2\). Thus the constant terms from the conditional squares are exactly \(E(G_n+n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})^2\).

The repeated-edge term \(R_n\) groups into independent centered functions of \(Z_s\). The conditional-second-moment \(L^2\) bound after (10), the \(O(m^{-1})\) edge coefficients, and the \(O(m)\) future edges give
\[
ER_n^2\lesssim\frac{M_n^2}{m}. \tag{20}
\]
For \(T_n\), regroup first over the unordered pair \((s,t)\). Pair kernels with disjoint edge sets are independent, and those sharing only one vertex are orthogonal by canonicality. A surviving repeated pair is the four-cycle contraction in (11); summation over possible common terminal vertices has total coefficient \(O(m^{-1})\). Since there are \(O(m^2)\) pairs,
\[
ET_n^2\lesssim m^2m^{-2}\operatorname{tr}(K^4)\lesssim M_n. \tag{21}
\]
For the mixed contraction, put \(u_r=E\{Z_r\ell_{n,r}(W_r)\}\). Covariance Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\|\Gamma_{a_r}^{-1/2}u_r\|_2^2\le E\ell_{n,r}^2,
\]
with the inverse understood on the covariance range. Moreover,
\[
\|\Gamma_a^{1/2}B\Gamma_b^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le\|\Gamma^{1/2}B\Gamma^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=\|K\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim1,
\]
because \(0\preceq\Gamma_a,\Gamma_b\preceq\Gamma\). Regrouping \(C_n\) over \(s\), applying Cauchy--Schwarz to its \(O(m)\) future indices, and then using independence of the resulting centered functions of \(Z_s\) proves
\[
EC_n^2\lesssim EG_n^2=O(S_n^2). \tag{22}
\]
Equations (20)--(22), \((x+y+z)^2\le3(x^2+y^2+z^2)\), \(S_n^4\ge A^4\asymp M_n^2\), and \(S_n^2\gtrsim M_n\) now give
\[
\frac{E\left[\left\{\sum_rE(\mathcal D_{n,r}^2\mid\mathcal F_{r-1})
-E(G_n+n\mathbb U_{J_y,J_z,n})^2\right\}^2\right]}{S_n^4}
\lesssim m^{-1}+\frac{M_n}{m^2}+M_n^{-1}+o(1)\longrightarrow0. \tag{23}
\]
Equations (1)--(23) establish the claimed noncompact Gram-inverse localization, both conjugations, fourth moments, maximal influence, repeated-edge, shared-vertex, four-cycle and mixed contractions, Lindeberg condition, and predictable-variance concentration.

Put \(a_y=\min\{s_y,1\}\) and \(e=\beta/(2\beta+1)=\{2+s_y^{-1}+ds_z^{-1}\}^{-1}\). For \(d\ge1\), the corrected full-minus-projected pilot-error term is bounded by
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\{2^{-(s_y+1)J_y}+2^{-s_zJ_z}\}.
\]
Balancing its covariate component with \(A_{J_y,J_z,n}/n\asymp2^{dJ_z/2}/n\), and then making the outcome component of the same order, gives exactly
\[
2^{J_z^*}\asymp\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2/(2s_z+d)},
\qquad
2^{J_y^*}\asymp\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2s_z/\{(s_y+1)(2s_z+d)\}},
\]
with optimized scale
\[
n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}.
\]
The corresponding projection dimension is \(o(n^2)\).  Moreover,
\[
e<\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d}<\frac{2s_z}{4s_z+d},
\]
and hence, including the positive logarithmic power in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\),
\[
\frac{n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}}{n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus there is no smoothness region in which the corrected certified Gram envelope is uniformly absorbed into \(\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}\); the earlier pilot-feasibility region disappears once the actual pilot-error Hessian gap is retained.

For every fixed \(0<\tau<\min\{s_y,s_z\}\), the explicit median-aggregated SmoothCOT estimator satisfies, uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)\),
\[
\left\{E(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n)^2\right\}^{1/2}
\lesssim_\tau n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau},
\qquad a_\tau=\frac{\tau}{2\tau+d+1}.
\]
When \(s_z\ge1\), the median-aggregated direct-COT estimator satisfies
\[
\left\{E(\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{dir,med}}-\theta_n)^2\right\}^{1/2}
\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{1+1/(d+2)}.
\]
Accordingly, the certified upper bracket is the deterministic minimum of the zero-estimator, corrected Gram, SmoothCOT, and applicable direct-COT envelopes.  The two global envelopes may sharpen the upper side, but \(a_\tau<\min\{4s_z/(4s_z+d),1/2\}\) and, when \(s_z\ge1\), \(1/(d+2)<\min\{4s_z/(4s_z+d),1/2\}\), so neither proves the intrinsic quadratic exponent.
statements.justification: This proposition explicitly optimizes the corrected pilot-error projection term and records the honest global fallback estimators.
statements.gap: The optimized observable Gram scale is provably slower than the intrinsic quadratic lower exponent for every finite positive smoothness pair.
statements.consumer: The minimax bracket and calibration-width question use the corrected resolutions and no longer advertise a nonexistent uniform absorption region.
statements.proof_tex:
Put
\[
e=\frac{\beta}{2\beta+1}
=\frac{1}{2+s_y^{-1}+ds_z^{-1}},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}=(\log n/n)^e.
\]
The exact von Mises identity and norm bound in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}observable\text{-}pilot\text{-}control}\) show that the full-minus-projected pilot-error contribution is
\[
O_{L^2}\!\left[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}
\{2^{-(s_y+1)J_y}+2^{-s_zJ_z}\}
\right],                                                    \tag{1}
\]
with the sign and additional higher-order terms stated there.  In particular, the true-discrepancy gaps \(B^y_{J_y,n}\) and \(B^z_{J_z,n}\) are not estimator biases.  By
\(\mathrm{prop{:}anisotropic\text{-}spectrum\text{-}bias}\),
\[
\frac{A_{J_y,J_z,n}}n\asymp\frac{2^{dJ_z/2}}n.             \tag{2}
\]
Writing \(x=2^{J_z}\), balance the covariate term in (1) with (2):
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}x^{-s_z}
=n^{-1}x^{d/2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x^{s_z+d/2}=n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{J_z^*}\asymp
\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2/(2s_z+d)}.           \tag{3}
\]
Equating the outcome term in (1) to this common scale gives
\[
2^{-(s_y+1)J_y^*}=2^{-s_zJ_z^*},
\qquad
2^{J_y^*}\asymp
\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2s_z/\{(s_y+1)(2s_z+d)\}}. \tag{4}
\]
Substitution into either side of the balance proves that the optimized scale is
\[
n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}.                 \tag{5}
\]
Since \(D_{J_y,J_z}\asymp2^{J_y+dJ_z}\), (3)--(4) yield
\[
D_{J_y^*,J_z^*}
=\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{\kappa+o(1)},
\qquad
\kappa=\frac{2s_z/(s_y+1)+2d}{2s_z+d}.                     \tag{6}
\]
Now \(s_y>0\) implies
\(2s_z/(s_y+1)<4s_z\), so \(\kappa<2\).  Since
\(n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}<n\) eventually, (6) proves
\(D_{J_y^*,J_z^*}=o(n^2)\).

Next,
\[
2+s_y^{-1}+ds_z^{-1}>2+ds_z^{-1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e<\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d}.
\]
For \(d>0\), cross-multiplication gives
\[
\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d}<\frac{2s_z}{4s_z+d}.                    \tag{7}
\]
The polynomial exponent in (5) is
\((2s_z+ed)/(2s_z+d)\).  Therefore
\[
\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d}-\frac{2s_z+ed}{2s_z+d}
=\frac{d\{2s_z-e(4s_z+d)\}}
{(4s_z+d)(2s_z+d)}>0,                                       \tag{8}
\]
where positivity follows from the second inequality in (7).  Restoring the positive logarithmic factor in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\), (8) proves
\[
\frac{n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}}
{n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}}\longrightarrow\infty.                 \tag{9}
\]
Consequently no positive finite pair \((s_y,s_z)\) makes the certified Gram scale uniformly absorbable into the intrinsic quadratic scale.

The remaining candidates are direct consequences of their established estimator lemmas.  Specifically,
\(\mathrm{lem{:}anisotropic\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}median\text{-}envelope}\) gives, for every fixed \(0<\tau<\min\{s_y,s_z\}\),
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n\|_2
\lesssim_\tau n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau},
\qquad a_\tau=\frac{\tau}{2\tau+d+1}.                    \tag{10}
\]
When \(s_z\ge1\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}direct\text{-}cot\text{-}median\text{-}envelope}\) gives
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{n,d}(s_y,s_z,\rho)}
\|\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{dir,med}}-\theta_n\|_2
\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{1+1/(d+2)}.                 \tag{11}
\]
The zero-estimator guarantee follows from the energy comparison in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}conditional\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\), and the Gram guarantee follows from
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\text{-}second\text{-}order\text{-}expansion}\) together with (3)--(5).  Selecting before observing the data the smallest deterministic guarantee among these explicit maps proves the certified upper minimum.

Finally, monotonicity of \(x/(2x+d+1)\) and \(\tau<s_z\) imply
\[
a_\tau<\frac{s_z}{2s_z+d+1}
<\min\left\{\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d},\frac12\right\}.          \tag{12}
\]
If \(s_z\ge1\) and \(d\ge1\), direct cross-multiplication gives
\[
\frac1{d+2}<\min\left\{\frac{4s_z}{4s_z+d},\frac12\right\}. \tag{13}
\]
Equations (1)--(13) prove the optimization, dimension condition, strict Gram gap, both fallback envelopes, and their stated failure to certify the intrinsic quadratic exponent.

statements.justification: Under explicitly fixed boundary-wavelet bases of regularity greater than \(\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\), this transfer corollary makes the existing sign-mixture converse and observable SmoothCOT envelope available on a recognizable fixed-radius positive isotropic scalar class.
statements.gap: The published SmoothCOT bound has a law-dependent constant and supplies no equality-local minimax converse; the transfer uniformizes that constant on the fixed \((\gamma,H)\) slice and adds the quadratic-and-zero sign-mixture lower benchmark, with the required wavelet regularity now explicit.
statements.consumer: Applied scalar SmoothCOT analyses with fixed boundary wavelets of regularity greater than \(\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\) can use the displayed bracket without claiming a matched quadratic rate or an observable mixed-regime confidence procedure.
statements.proof_tex:
Put \(s=\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\) and \(a_\tau=\tau/(2\tau+d+1)\).  The theorem-level premise fixes compactly supported boundary-corrected bases \(\Psi_y\) and \(\Psi_z\), each with regularity strictly greater than \(s\).  Thus every boundary-wavelet approximation and H\"older characterization below is licensed for all fixed \(0<\tau<s\).  We first prove the upper inequality uniformly over the entire class \(\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}(s,H,\gamma,\rho)\).

First dispose of the boundary value \(\rho=0\).  For any class member, integrating the Neumann equation exactly as in (5) below gives
\[
\rho_n^2=\int_{\mathcal Z_d}\int_0^1
\frac{\left\{\int_0^y\Delta_n(v,z)\,dv\right\}^2}{\bar q_n(y,z)}\,dy\,dR_n(z).
\]
The integrand is nonnegative and \(\bar q_n>0\).  Thus \(\rho_n=0\) implies \(\int_0^y\Delta_n(v,z)\,dv=0\) for Lebesgue-almost every \((y,z)\); continuity of the class densities and differentiation in \(y\) then imply \(\Delta_n=0\) everywhere.  Hence \(Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z)=Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\), \(\theta_n=0\), and the zero estimator has zero risk.  Both sides of the claimed bracket are zero.  We may therefore assume \(0<\rho\le\rho_{\mathrm{adm}}\) for the remaining construction.

For any member and either arm, integration of the joint-density bounds in \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}isotropic\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}local\text{-}slice}\) over the unit outcome interval gives
\[
\gamma^{-1}\le r_n(z)=\int_0^1p_{a,n}(y,z)\,dy\le\gamma. \tag{1}
\]
Consequently the conditional densities defined in that same definition satisfy
\[
\gamma^{-2}\le q_{a,n}(y,z)=\frac{p_{a,n}(y,z)}{r_n(z)}\le\gamma^2,
\qquad
\gamma^{-2}\le\bar q_n(y,z)\le\gamma^2. \tag{2}
\]
Every division in (2) is licensed by the positive lower bound in (1).

Let \(F_{a,z}(y)=\int_0^yq_{a,n}(v,z)\,dv\), let \(Q_{a,z}=F_{a,z}^{-1}\), and put \(H_z=F_{1,z}-F_{0,z}\).  Strict positivity in (2) makes both inverses well defined.  The scalar increasing-rearrangement identity used in \(\mathrm{thm{:}conditional\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\) is
\[
W_2^2\{Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\}
=\int_0^1\{Q_{1,z}(u)-Q_{0,z}(u)\}^2\,du. \tag{3}
\]
If \(u=F_{0,z}(y)\), the mean-value theorem supplies a point \(\zeta_{y,z}\) between \(Q_{0,z}(u)=y\) and \(Q_{1,z}(u)\) such that
\[
H_z(y)=q_{1,n}(\zeta_{y,z},z)\{Q_{0,z}(u)-Q_{1,z}(u)\}. \tag{4}
\]
On the other hand, integrating the defining Neumann equation for \(\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n\), using zero conditional mass and the two Neumann boundary conditions, and then integrating by parts gives
\[
\int_0^1\Delta_n(y,z)\{\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n(\cdot,z)\}(y)\,dy
=\int_0^1\frac{H_z(y)^2}{\bar q_n(y,z)}\,dy. \tag{5}
\]
Changing variables in (3), then applying (2) to (4)--(5), yields
\[
W_2^2\{Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\}
\le\gamma^8\int_0^1\Delta_n(y,z)\{\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n(\cdot,z)\}(y)\,dy. \tag{6}
\]
The common marginal in the slice definition permits integration against the single measure \(R_n\).  Since \(\rho_n\le\rho\), (6) proves
\[
0\le\theta_n\le\gamma^8\rho_n^2\le\gamma^8\rho^2. \tag{7}
\]
Therefore the zero estimator has uniform root-mean-square error at most \(\gamma^8\rho^2\).

We next control the observable SmoothCOT estimator on the whole slice.  Fix \(0<\tau<s\) and set
\[
\epsilon_\tau=\frac{s-\tau}{2}>0,
\qquad
\alpha_\tau=\tau+\epsilon_\tau=\frac{s+\tau}{2}<s. \tag{8}
\]
On the fixed cube, the definition of the H\"older norm directly implies the continuous embedding from \(\mathcal C^s\) into \(\mathcal C^{\alpha_\tau}\): derivatives through order \(\lfloor\alpha_\tau\rfloor\) and the required difference quotients are among those controlled by the \(\mathcal C^s\) norm.  Hence the slice condition gives
\[
\sup_{a,n}\|p_{a,n}\|_{\mathcal C^{\alpha_\tau}([0,1]^{d+1})}
\le C_{s,d,\tau}H. \tag{9}
\]
Together, the joint positivity in the slice definition and (9) verify the hypotheses of \(\mathrm{lem{:}lin\text{-}gao\text{-}blanchet\text{-}glynn\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}rate}\), with source smoothness \(\tau\) and extra smoothness \(\epsilon_\tau\).  Its printed constant is law-dependent, so the desired uniformity does not follow from the citation alone; we now verify that every law-dependent input used by that result is uniformly bounded by the fixed \((\gamma,H)\) envelope and the fixed bases.

Let \(N=N_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\), let \(J=\lfloor\log_2N/(2\tau+d+1)\rfloor\), and let \(\widetilde p_{a,J}\) be the empirical boundary-wavelet projection in one paired block.  The theorem-level basis premise permits the boundary-wavelet characterization of the H\"older bound (9).  Orthonormality, the resulting coefficient decay, coefficient variances bounded by \(p_{a,n}\le\gamma\), and the fixed compact-support overlap number give
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}}
E_P\|\widetilde p_{a,J}-p_{a,n}\|_2^2
\le C_{s,d,\tau,\gamma,H,\Psi_y,\Psi_z}
\left\{2^{-2\alpha_\tau J}+\frac{2^{(d+1)J}}{N}\right\}
\lesssim N^{-2a_\tau}. \tag{10}
\]
For the same reason, bounded-summand exponential Markov bounds applied coefficientwise, followed by a union bound over \(O\{2^{(d+1)J}\}\) coefficients and the compact-overlap inequality, give
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}}
P\!\left(\|\widetilde p_{a,J}-p_{a,n}\|_\infty>\frac{1}{2\gamma}\right)
\le C_{s,d,\tau,\gamma,H,\Psi_y,\Psi_z}N^{-2} \tag{11}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Indeed, the deterministic sup-norm bias is \(O(2^{-\alpha_\tau J})\), while the stochastic scale is
\[
O\!\left[\left\{J2^{(d+1)J}/N\right\}^{1/2}\right]
=O\{J^{1/2}N^{-a_\tau}\}=o(1).
\]
Thus the positive-part normalization in \(\mathrm{def{:}smoothcot\text{-}median\text{-}estimator}\) is inactive with the uniform probability in (11), and every reciprocal-density constant on that event is bounded by a fixed power of \(\gamma\).

For clarity, the comparison of the estimated aligned marginal with the common true marginal also has a law-uniform form.  If \(f(z)=W_2^2\{Q_{0,n}(\cdot\mid z),Q_{1,n}(\cdot\mid z)\}\), if \(\widehat f\) is its block analogue, and if \(\widehat r\) is the pooled block marginal, then the outcome diameter is one and hence
\[
\left|\int\widehat f\,\widehat r-\int f r_n\right|
\le\|\widehat r-r_n\|_1
+2\sum_{a=0}^1\int W_1(\widehat Q_a^z,Q_a^z)\widehat r(z)\,dz. \tag{12}
\]
The first term is bounded by the two joint \(L^2\) errors in (10).  The second is the conditional negative-order term in the cited SmoothCOT argument.  The fixed reciprocal bound, (9)--(11), and (12) are precisely the fixed-ball wavelet-risk, positivity-event, reciprocal-density, and alternative-marginal ingredients tracked in \(\mathrm{lem{:}anisotropic\text{-}smoothcot\text{-}median\text{-}envelope}\).  Consequently the cited block conclusion is uniformized to
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}(s,H,\gamma,\rho)}
E_P\left|\widehat V_{\ell,\tau,n}^{\mathrm{sm}}-\theta_n\right|
\le C_{s,d,\tau,\gamma,H,\Psi_y,\Psi_z}N^{-a_\tau}. \tag{13}
\]
This step applies to every member of the declared slice, not only to the lower-bound family.

Put \(\delta_N=C_{s,d,\tau,\gamma,H,\Psi_y,\Psi_z}N^{-a_\tau}\).  Markov's inequality applied to (13) shows that a block is bad at threshold \(8\delta_N\) with probability at most \(1/8\).  The product sampling experiment in the slice definition makes the paired blocks independent.  If their median is bad, at least half the blocks are bad, so
\[
P\!\left(
|\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n|>8\delta_N
\right)
\le2^{K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}}8^{-(K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}+1)/2}
\le2^{-K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}/2}. \tag{14}
\]
Choose the fixed multiplier in \(K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\asymp\log n\) so that the last expression is at most \(\delta_N^2\).  Both the estimator and \(\theta_n\) lie in \([0,1]\); therefore
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}}
E_P(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}-\theta_n)^2
\le64\delta_N^2+2^{-K_n^{\mathrm{sm}}/2}
\le65\delta_N^2. \tag{15}
\]
Since \(N_n^{\mathrm{sm}}\asymp n/\log n\), (15) proves the uniform SmoothCOT root-mean-square bound \(C_{\mathrm{sm},\tau}n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau}\).  The constant depends only on the fixed quantities listed in the proposition, including the fixed boundary-wavelet constants, and is independent of \(n,\rho\), and the model element.  Selecting before observing the data whichever of the zero estimator and the median SmoothCOT estimator has the smaller deterministic guarantee in (7) and (15) proves the upper inequality.

We finally prove the lower inequality by embedding the explicit hard subclass.  In \(\mathrm{def{:}rademacher\text{-}family}\), set its covariate smoothness parameter to \(s_z=s=\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\), choose
\[
2^{J_z}\asymp n^{2/(4s+d)},
\qquad
b_{n,\omega}(z)=\gamma_n\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_{J_z}}\omega_k\psi^z_{J_z,k}(z),
\]
and use \(r_n\equiv1\) and
\[
p_{a,n,\omega}(y,z)=q_{a,n,\omega}^{\mathrm{lb}}(y,z)
=1+(2a-1)b_{n,\omega}(z)\cos(2\pi y)/2. \tag{16}
\]
The support in (16) is the required scalar-outcome cube, and \(\int_0^1\cos(2\pi y)\,dy=0\), so both covariate marginals are the common uniform density.  Because \(\Psi_z\) has regularity strictly greater than \(s\), its level-\(J_z\) scaling law and the disjoint supports in \(\mathcal K_{J_z}\), together with the amplitude in \(\mathrm{def{:}rademacher\text{-}family}\), give exactly the calculation recorded in \(\mathrm{lem{:}explicit\text{-}mixture\text{-}checks}\):
\[
\|b_{n,\omega}\|_\infty\le C_1c_0 2^{-sJ_z},
\qquad
\|b_{n,\omega}\|_{\mathcal C^s([0,1]^d)}\le C_2c_0. \tag{17}
\]
Because the outcome factor in (16) is fixed and smooth, the product rule for isotropic H\"older norms and (17) imply
\[
\|p_{a,n,\omega}-1\|_{\mathcal C^s([0,1]^{d+1})}
\le C_3c_0. \tag{18}
\]
The slack \(H-\|1\|_{\mathcal C^s}>0\) is fixed.  Choose the single constant \(c_0>0\) so small that \(C_3c_0\le H-\|1\|_{\mathcal C^s}\) and that the pointwise perturbation in (16) is at most \(\min\{1-\gamma^{-1},\gamma-1\}\).  Equations (17)--(18) then give, uniformly in \(n,\rho\), and \(\omega\),
\[
\gamma^{-1}\le p_{a,n,\omega}\le\gamma,
\qquad
\|p_{a,n,\omega}\|_{\mathcal C^s}\le H. \tag{19}
\]
Thus positivity and the fixed isotropic radius are verified with constants independent of the model element.

For (16), \(\bar q_n=1\), \(\Delta_n=b_{n,\omega}\cos(2\pi y)\), and direct solution of the Neumann equation gives
\[
\mathcal G_{n,z}\Delta_n(\cdot,z)
=\frac{b_{n,\omega}(z)}{4\pi^2}\cos(2\pi y).
\]
Orthonormality of the selected covariate wavelets and the radius branch of \(\gamma_n\) therefore yield
\[
\rho_n^2
=\frac{\gamma_n^2M_{J_z}}{8\pi^2}
\le\frac{c_0^2}{8\pi^2}\rho^2
\le\rho^2. \tag{20}
\]
Together, (16), (19), and (20) prove that the null and every sign-paired alternative lie in \(\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}(s,H,\gamma,\rho)\).  This verifies class containment directly; it is not inferred merely from the hard-family definition.

The endpoint and mixture calculations in \(\mathrm{lem{:}explicit\text{-}mixture\text{-}checks}\), based on the second variation in \(\mathrm{lem{:}cosine\text{-}second\text{-}variation}\), give
\[
\theta_{n,\omega}-\theta_{n,0}
\ge c_4\gamma_n^2M_{J_z}
\asymp c_0^2\min\!\left\{\rho^2,n^{-4s/(4s+d)}\right\} \tag{21}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\), while
\[
\chi^2(\overline{\mathbb P}_n,\mathbb P_n^0)
\le\exp\{C_\chi n^2\gamma_n^4M_{J_z}\}-1
\le\eta \tag{22}
\]
for a fixed \(\eta<1\) after decreasing the same fixed \(c_0\).  This choice is uniform because, at the displayed resolution, \(n^2\gamma_n^4M_{J_z}=O(c_0^4)\).  Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the mixture likelihood ratio gives
\[
\|\overline{\mathbb P}_n-\mathbb P_n^0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le\frac12\sqrt\eta<1. \tag{23}
\]
Threshold any estimator halfway between the null endpoint and the common lower separation in (21).  On either testing error its absolute estimation error is at least half that separation.  Averaging over the Rademacher alternatives and applying (23), as in the mixture testing argument of \(\mathrm{thm{:}conditional\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\), gives
\[
\inf_{\widetilde\theta_n}
\sup_{P\in\{\mathbb P_n^0\}\cup\{\mathbb P_{n,\omega}:\omega\}}
\{E_P(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_n)^2\}^{1/2}
\ge c_5\min\!\left\{\rho^2,n^{-4s/(4s+d)}\right\}. \tag{24}
\]
The set in (24) is a subclass of the full slice by (16)--(20), so its minimax lower bound transfers upward.  Substituting \(s=\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\) completes the lower inequality.  No fixed-frequency regular witness was used, so (24) justifies only the stated quadratic-and-zero lower benchmark and not a \(\rho n^{-1/2}\) term.  The upper and lower exponents need not agree, which proves the asserted honest unmatched bracket.

sampling_model.design: Two independent randomized treatment-arm samples, each of even size \(n=2m\), with deterministic equal folds of size \(m\).
sampling_model.units: Observations are \(W_{a,i,n}=(Y_{a,i,n},Z_{a,i,n})\), with scalar outcome support \([0,1]\) and covariate support \([0,1]^d\).
sampling_model.treatment: Randomized arm membership directly samples the two potential-outcome marginals.
sampling_model.overlap: Propensity overlap is not used; the arm laws share the marginal \(R_n\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: For \(d\ge1\), opposite-fold joint and marginal wavelet projections are conditionally normalized and clipped to fixed positive bounds. Their averaged conditional density enters a zero-outcome-mean ridge Galerkin inverse, which defines the observed Hessian, first-order score, diagonal-free kernel, and foldwise variance estimator even off the clipping-inactive event. For \(d=0\), the separate branch uses the full empirical quantile processes.

estimand_functional:
Put \(a_y=\min\{s_y,1\}\). For \(d\ge1\), use the corrected pilot-error balancing resolutions
\[
2^{J_z^*}\asymp\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2/(2s_z+d)},
\qquad
2^{J_y^*}\asymp\{n\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}\}^{2s_z/\{(s_y+1)(2s_z+d)\}}.
\]
The explicit Gram-corrected estimator \(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{an}}_{J_y^*,J_z^*,n}\) has local RMSE at most
\[
\rho n^{-1/2}
+n^{-2s_z/(2s_z+d)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{d/(2s_z+d)}
+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^{2+a_y}
+\rho^{2a_y/(2+3/s_y+d/s_z)}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^2.
\]
For every fixed \(0<\tau<\min\{s_y,s_z\}\), the explicit median-aggregated aligned wavelet estimator \(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{sm,med}}_{\tau,n}\) has RMSE \(O_\tau\{n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau}\}\), where \(a_\tau=\tau/(2\tau+d+1)\). When \(s_z\ge1\), \(\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{dir,med}}\) additionally has RMSE \(O\{n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{1+1/(d+2)}\}\). The certified upper map is the deterministic minimum of these guarantees and the zero-estimator guarantee \(O(\rho^2)\). The sign mixture and fixed-frequency two-point construction give the intrinsic lower frontier
\[
\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}\}.
\]
The optimized observable Gram scale is strictly slower than \(n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}\), so the conditional result is an honest two-sided bracket rather than a matched rate in the nontrivial quadratic zone.  The quantities \(B^y_{J_y,n}\) and \(B^z_{J_z,n}\) are true-discrepancy energy-approximation gaps and are not estimator biases or centering terms. For \(d=0\), \(\widehat\theta^0_{J_y^0,n}\) has local RMSE \(\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-1}\}\)

Fix the compactly supported boundary-corrected bases \(\Psi_y\) and \(\Psi_z\) used below with regularity strictly greater than \(\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\). On the additional recognizable positive isotropic slice \(\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}(\beta_{\mathrm{iso}},H,\gamma,\rho)\), for every fixed \(0<\tau<\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}\), the same causal endpoint obeys the transferred minimax root-mean-square bracket
\[
c_{\mathrm{sm}}\min\!\left\{\rho^2,n^{-4\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}/(4\beta_{\mathrm{iso}}+d)}\right\}
\le \inf_{\widetilde\theta_n}\sup_{P\in\mathcal S^{\mathrm{sm}}_{n,d}}
\{E_P(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_n)^2\}^{1/2}
\le C_{\mathrm{sm},\tau}\min\!\left\{\rho^2,n^{-a_\tau}(\log n)^{a_\tau}\right\}.
\]
The upper side uses the existing zero and median-aggregated aligned wavelet SmoothCOT estimators; the quadratic-and-zero lower side uses the existing sign-paired family. This broader-class bracket is not asserted to be tight in its nontrivial quadratic zone.

tldr: For \(d\ge1\), conditional squared Wasserstein distance has an anisotropic boundary geometry: inverse ellipticity smooths outcome frequencies while covariate resolution replicates the ordered spectrum. A min--max comparison gives Hilbert--Schmidt norm \(\asymp2^{dJ_z/2}\), outcome bias \(2^{-2(s_y+1)J_y}\), and covariate bias \(2^{-2s_zJ_z}\). A fully observed two-fold statistic uses clipped-and-normalized opposite-fold density pilots, a ridge Galerkin inverse, explicit first-order scores, and a diagonal-free second-order kernel. In the pilot-feasible smoothness region, balancing the three scales yields local rate \(\min\{\rho^2,\rho n^{-1/2}+n^{-4s_z/(4s_z+d)}\}\) and elbow \(s_z=d/4\), matched by the sign-paired converse; the limit statement is an \(n\)-dependent Gaussian-quadratic approximation, with chaos only under \(\ell^2\) spectral convergence. The separate \(d=0\) branch recovers the two-sample del Barrio--Gin\'e--Utzet law and \(n^{-1}\) scale. Uniform mixed-regime calibration remains open.

project_justification.gap: SmoothCOT Section 3.3, Theorem 3.2, Remark 3.2, and Appendix C.4 stop at a regular CLT and faster-than-root-\(n\) equality statement. Existing unconditional Wasserstein laws, changing-kernel theory, fixed-entropic causal transport, and the direct-estimation COT abstract do not provide a verified observable equality-local anisotropic frontier.
project_justification.niche: The missing object is a primitive smoothness-by-equality frontier that separates outcome elliptic smoothing from covariate rank and also recovers the unconditional \(d=0\) benchmark with the correct estimator and constants.
project_justification.fill: The project derives canonical ordered-spectrum and bias bounds, constructs the foldwise clipped ridge-Galerkin statistic, states the normalized triangular experiment and regular studentization with exact split constants, matches the pilot-feasible rate using a checked sign-paired wavelet family, and isolates honest all-regime calibration as the unresolved node.

related_work: Lin, Gao, Blanchet, and Glynn's SmoothCOT Section 3.3 gives quadratic stability, Theorem 3.2 gives the regular Gaussian law, Remark 3.2 records faster-than-root-\(n\) convergence at equality, and Appendix C.4 proves the CLT; the mixed triangular theorem strictly tightens that scalar randomized-arm specialization. Their AISTATS 2026 paper, verified only through its arXiv abstract and proceedings metadata, advertises a direct consistent nonparametric conditional-OT value estimator and a convergence rate. Formula-level overlap with the equality-local frontier remains externally unverifiable because its proceedings theorem text was inaccessible, so it is treated only as informing the project. Goldman, Huesmann, and Otto motivate inverse-elliptic linearization. Robins, Li, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and van der Vaart inform changing-kernel approximation. Del Barrio, Gin\'e, and Utzet provide the weighted quantile-process law recovered by the separate \(d=0\) branch. Chen and Fang motivate derivative-aware calibration, and Sturma, Drton, and Leung inform multiplier coupling. Agarwal and Luedtke analyze fixed-entropic causal transport. Niles-Weed and Berthet provide negative-order wavelet geometry; Manole and Niles-Weed provide unconditional separation-sensitive rates. Goldfeld, Kato, Nietert, and Rioux treat fixed Gaussian smoothing. Neykov, Wasserman, Kim, and Balakrishnan develop multiresolution conditional Wasserstein testing. Bickel and Ritov and Ingster and Suslina inform the explicit sign-mixture converse.
technical_internal_limitation: The cosine witness reduces one lower-bound channel to a covariate quadratic functional, but the observable upper expansion still requires uniform control of a density-dependent ridge Galerkin inverse. The optimal sup-norm pilot rate makes the advertised \(s_z\)-driven upper frontier available only when \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pil},n}^3=o(r_{n,d}(s_z))\). Full operator-norm covariance estimation additionally requires \(D_{J_y,J_z}\log n=o(m)\) and is used only for an observed spectral proxy, not for the point estimator.
honest_scope: The model has scalar compactly supported outcomes, equal randomized arm sizes, a shared covariate marginal, positive anisotropic H\"older densities, and known smoothness. The sharp conditional upper and lower frontier is stated for \(d\ge1\) only in the explicit pilot-feasible region; outside it the Rademacher lower bound remains, but no observable upper rate is claimed. The primary limit result is triangular, and a fixed Gaussian-chaos limit requires \(\ell^2\) convergence of normalized spectra and shifts. The \(d=0\) result uses a separate full-sample empirical-quantile branch. Adaptation, multivariate outcomes, observational propensity estimation, observed spectral plug-in at high dimension, and uniform mixed calibration are open.
